What is the difference between a cold and the flu?

Colds and the flu are both respiratory illnesses but caused by different viruses. Colds usually start gradually with a runny nose, sneezing and a mild sore throat, and rarely cause fever. The flu comes on suddenly with fever, chills, body aches, tiredness and a dry cough, and can keep you in bed for several days. Flu symptoms tend to be more intense and carry a higher risk of complications such as pneumonia, especially in older adults, young children and people with chronic conditions.

How effective is the annual flu vaccine?

The annual flu vaccine is the best single protection against influenza. Effectiveness varies year to year because the vaccine is redesigned each season to match circulating strains; it typically reduces the risk of illness by around 40-60% in the general population when strains match well. Even when you catch the flu after vaccination, the vaccine lowers the chance of severe illness, hospitalisation and death. Immunity takes about two weeks to build after the shot, which is why early-season vaccination is recommended.

When should I stay home from work or school if I am sick?

Stay home while you have a fever and for at least 24 hours after the fever ends without using fever-reducing medicine. If you have vomiting or diarrhoea, stay home until those symptoms have stopped for at least 24 hours, because you remain contagious during that window. Going back early risks infecting colleagues and classmates and slows your own recovery. If you work with vulnerable groups such as infants, older adults or immunocompromised patients, be even more conservative about returning.

Is it safe to exercise when I have a cold?

Mild to moderate exercise is generally safe if your symptoms are above the neck, such as a runny nose, nasal congestion or a mild sore throat, and you feel well enough. Reduce intensity and stop if you feel worse. Do not exercise if you have below-the-neck symptoms like chest tightness, a hacking cough, body aches, fever or fatigue, because exercising with a systemic illness can raise the risk of myocarditis and prolong recovery. When in doubt, rest for a few days; missing one week of training costs far less than a complication.

What does drinking water actually do for the body?

Water supports nearly every bodily process. It carries nutrients and oxygen in the blood, removes waste through urine and sweat, cushions joints, protects sensitive tissue, and regulates body temperature through sweating and breathing. Even mild dehydration of one to two percent of body weight can reduce concentration, mood and physical performance. Plain water is the best default drink for hydration; sugary drinks add calories without extra benefit.

How much sleep do adults really need?

Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep per night for good health. Sleeping less than seven hours on a regular basis is linked to weight gain, impaired memory and concentration, weakened immunity, and higher risks of high blood pressure, diabetes and heart disease. Sleep quality matters as much as quantity: a regular schedule, a dark quiet room, and no screens right before bed all help. If you regularly wake up tired despite enough hours in bed, discuss it with a healthcare provider.

Why is smoking so harmful even in small amounts?

There is no safe level of smoking. Each cigarette delivers thousands of chemicals, at least seventy of which are known carcinogens. Even light or occasional smoking damages blood vessels, raises blood pressure and heart rate, and reduces lung function. Second-hand smoke exposes non-smokers, especially children, to the same toxic mix and increases their risk of asthma attacks, ear infections and sudden infant death syndrome. The good news is that quitting pays off quickly: heart rate and carbon monoxide levels normalise within days and lung function improves within months.

What counts as a fever, and when is it dangerous?

A fever is a temporary rise in body temperature, usually defined as 38 degrees Celsius or 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit or higher. It is most often a normal immune response to infection and by itself is not dangerous. Seek medical care urgently if the fever is above 40 degrees Celsius, lasts more than three days, or comes with a stiff neck, confusion, difficulty breathing, a rash that does not fade under pressure, severe dehydration, or if the patient is an infant under three months. For ordinary fevers, rest, fluids and fever-reducing medicine as directed are usually enough.

Do I need to take vitamins if I eat a balanced diet?

If you eat a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein sources, you usually do not need a daily multivitamin. Supplements make sense for specific, confirmed deficiencies or life stages: folic acid when planning pregnancy, vitamin B12 for strict vegans and older adults with poor absorption, vitamin D in regions with little winter sun, and iron when a test shows a deficiency. More is not better: high-dose supplements can be harmful, so treat them as medicine, not food.

How quickly do antibiotics work, and why must I finish the course?

Many bacterial infections start improving within one to three days of the right antibiotic, but this depends on the infection type and severity. You must finish the prescribed course even when you feel better, because surviving bacteria can regroup and cause a relapse, and incomplete courses contribute to antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics do nothing against viruses such as colds and flu; taking them then only adds side effects and resistance risk. Never use leftover antibiotics or someone else's prescription.

What is the correct way to wash my hands?

Wet your hands with clean running water, apply soap, and lather for at least twenty seconds, making sure to scrub the backs of your hands, between your fingers and under your nails, then rinse and dry with a clean towel. Twenty seconds is about the time it takes to hum the Happy Birthday song twice. Alcohol-based sanitiser with at least 60 percent alcohol is a good substitute when soap and water are unavailable, but it does not work well on visibly dirty hands or against some stomach viruses.

Is BMI a reliable measure of health?

BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, is a useful population-level screening tool but an imperfect individual one. A BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 is considered normal, 25 to 29.9 overweight and 30 or above obese. It does not distinguish muscle from fat, ignores fat distribution, and can misclassify athletes and older adults. Waist circumference and metabolic markers such as blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol give a fuller picture, so treat BMI as one signal among several rather than a verdict.

What are the main symptoms of dehydration?

Early signs of dehydration include thirst, dark yellow urine, urinating less than usual, dry mouth and lips, tiredness and a mild headache. As it worsens you may feel dizzy when standing, become irritable or confused, and stop sweating despite heat. Infants and older adults show signs later and dry out faster, so sunken eyes, no wet nappies for hours or sudden confusion in an elderly person should be taken seriously. The remedy is straightforward: drink fluids steadily, use oral rehydration solution after heavy fluid loss, and seek care if vomiting prevents drinking.

How can I lower my blood pressure without medication?

Lifestyle changes have a real, measurable effect on blood pressure. Reducing sodium towards under 2 grams per day, following a vegetable-and-fruit-rich pattern like the DASH diet, doing about 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise a week, limiting alcohol, quitting smoking, managing stress and sleeping seven-plus hours can together lower systolic pressure by several points. Losing even five percent of body weight helps if you are overweight. If your doctor has prescribed medication, keep taking it while you build these habits, and let them decide about tapering.

What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the body destroys the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas, so no insulin is made; it usually appears in childhood or adolescence and requires lifelong insulin. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body becomes resistant to insulin or the pancreas cannot produce enough; it is far more common, typically appears in adulthood, and is strongly linked to weight, inactivity and genetics. Type 2 can often be prevented or delayed with diet, exercise and weight management, while type 1 cannot currently be prevented. Both types need medical follow-up to prevent damage to eyes, kidneys, nerves and the heart.

How long am I contagious with the flu?

With influenza you are contagious from about one day before symptoms start until roughly five to seven days after they begin; children and people with weakened immune systems can spread the virus for longer. The virus travels in droplets from coughing, sneezing and talking, so stay home, cover coughs and wash hands often during that window. If you must be around others while recovering, a well-fitting mask reduces the spread. Fever usually signals the most contagious phase, which is why waiting 24 hours after the fever resolves is a sensible rule of thumb.

Are energy drinks safe for teenagers?

Energy drinks are not recommended for children and teenagers. A single can often contains 80 to 300 mg of caffeine plus high amounts of sugar, which can cause disturbed sleep, anxiety, a racing heart and higher blood pressure in young people, whose tolerance is lower than adults. Some teenagers mix them with exercise or alcohol, which increases the risks further. Water and, for older teens, moderate amounts of tea or coffee are far safer sources of alertness; the better fix for tiredness is sleep.

What is herd immunity and why does it matter?

Herd immunity happens when enough people in a community are immune to an infection that it can no longer spread easily, which indirectly protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns or people with certain medical conditions. For most diseases this threshold is reached through vaccination, not through mass infection, because letting a disease spread unchecked causes preventable deaths and long-term complications. The required coverage depends on how contagious the disease is; measles, for example, needs roughly 95 percent immunity because it is extremely contagious. When coverage drops, outbreaks return, which is why childhood vaccination rates are monitored so closely.

When is a sore throat something to worry about?

Most sore throats are caused by viruses, come with cold symptoms, and clear up within a week with fluids, warm salt-water gargles and paracetamol or ibuprofen. See a clinician if the pain is severe, lasts more than a week, or comes with a fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, difficulty swallowing or breathing, drooling, a muffled voice, white patches on the tonsils with swollen neck glands but no cough, or a fine sandpaper-like rash, because these suggest strep throat or an abscess that needs specific treatment. Strep throat is treated with antibiotics both to speed recovery and to prevent rheumatic fever.

Does stress really make you physically sick?

Yes. Chronic stress keeps the body flooded with cortisol and adrenaline, which over time suppresses immune defences, raises blood pressure and blood sugar, disturbs digestion and sleep, and increases muscle pain and headaches. People under long-term stress catch more colds, heal slower and are more prone to anxiety and depression. The most effective countermeasures are regular exercise, consistent sleep, social connection, limiting alcohol and caffeine, and deliberate relaxation practices such as slow breathing or mindfulness. If stress feels unmanageable or comes with persistent low mood, talking to a professional is a health decision, not a weakness.

What should I keep in a basic home first-aid kit?

A practical home kit covers cleaning, covering and comfort: sterile gauze and adhesive bandages in several sizes, medical tape, antiseptic solution or wipes, a digital thermometer, disposable gloves, scissors and tweezers, burn gel or dressings, saline for rinsing eyes or wounds, an elastic bandage for sprains, and pain relief such as paracetamol and ibuprofen. Add a week of any regular prescription medicines, and any emergency items your doctor recommends, such as an antihistamine or an epinephrine auto-injector if there are allergies in the family. Check the kit twice a year and replace anything expired.

How much exercise per week is enough?

The widely accepted guideline for adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity, such as brisk walking or cycling, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, such as running, spread across the week, plus muscle-strengthening exercise on two or more days. Moderate means you can talk but not sing; vigorous means talking in full sentences is hard. Even short bouts count, so three ten-minute walks a day are nearly as good as one thirty-minute session. Some activity is always better than none, so if you are starting from zero, a daily ten-minute walk already lowers your risk of heart disease, diabetes and depression.

What is antibiotic resistance and why should I care?

Antibiotic resistance happens when bacteria evolve to survive the drugs designed to kill them, often because antibiotics are used too often, at wrong doses, or stopped early. Resistant infections are harder and more expensive to treat, need longer hospital stays, and can turn simple procedures risky again. You help slow it by taking antibiotics only when a clinician prescribes them, finishing the course as directed, never sharing leftovers, and preventing infections in the first place with vaccination and hand hygiene. Surgery, chemotherapy and childbirth all rely on antibiotics still working, which is why this is a personal issue, not just a hospital one.

Is it dangerous to mix paracetamol and ibuprofen?

For most adults, taking paracetamol and ibuprofen together at correct doses is not dangerous and can even work better for some pain, because they act through different mechanisms. The rules that matter are: never exceed 3 grams of paracetamol per day from all sources unless a doctor advises otherwise, watch out for paracetamol hidden in cold-and-flu combination products, take ibuprofen with food and avoid it if you have kidney problems, ulcers or take blood thinners, and leave at least four to six hours between doses of the same drug. When unsure, ask a pharmacist; they answer this question daily.

What is hypertension and why is it called the silent killer?

Hypertension means persistently raised blood pressure, generally 140 over 90 mmHg or higher in a clinic, or 135 over 85 for home readings. It is called silent because it usually causes no symptoms while it quietly damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over years, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney failure. Because you cannot feel it, the only way to know is to measure it; adults should have it checked at least every one to two years, more often if readings are borderline. It responds well to treatment: medication plus less salt, more movement, weight control and limited alcohol.

Should I be worried about mold in my apartment?

You should take mold seriously without panicking. Mold needs moisture, so it signals a damp problem such as leaks, condensation or poor ventilation. Exposure can cause a blocked nose, throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and eye irritation, and it hits people with asthma, allergies or weakened immune systems hardest. Small patches on hard surfaces can be cleaned with detergent and water while wearing gloves and ventilating the room; never dry-brush mold, it releases spores. Anything larger than about one square metre, mold inside walls or returning growth needs professional assessment and fixing the moisture source, otherwise it grows back.

How do I know if a headache is an emergency?

Most headaches are tension or migraine and not dangerous, but a few red flags mean seek care immediately: a sudden worst-ever headache like a thunderclap, headache with fever plus a stiff neck, rash or confusion, weakness, numbness, slurred speech or vision loss, a headache that starts after a head injury, new headache patterns in someone over 50, or any headache that steadily worsens over days with nausea. For ordinary tension headaches, rest, hydration, stress management and simple painkillers usually suffice; see a doctor if they become frequent, meaning more than a few per month.

What is the best way to quit smoking?

The most successful approach combines behavioural support with medication. Set a quit date, remove cigarettes and lighters from your environment, and tell the people around you so they can support you. Nicotine replacement therapy, such as patches combined with gum or lozenges for breakthrough cravings, roughly doubles success rates; prescription medicines such as varenicline or bupropion help many people and are worth discussing with a doctor. Expect cravings to peak in the first week and fade over a month, and treat a slipped cigarette as data, not failure. Quitlines and free apps add structure and accountability.

Are e-cigarettes a safe way to quit smoking?

E-cigarettes are less harmful than continuing to smoke because they deliver nicotine without burning tobacco, which is what produces tar and most of the deadly carcinogens, and some smokers have used them to quit successfully. They are not harmless: the vapour irritates airways, the long-term effects are still unknown, and nicotine itself is addictive and raises blood pressure and heart rate. They should never be used by non-smokers, teenagers or pregnant women. If you use them to quit, aim to stop vaping too once you are safely off cigarettes, and consider first-line methods such as nicotine replacement therapy plus behavioural support.

What should I do in the first minutes of a suspected stroke?

Call emergency services immediately; stroke treatment is a race against time because brain tissue dies by the minute. While waiting, note the exact time symptoms started or were last seen normal, because clot-busting drugs work only within a few hours of that moment. Use the FAST check: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or numbness, Speech slurred or strange, Time to call. Do not give food, drink or aspirin, since some strokes are caused by bleeding and swallowing may be unsafe. Unlock the door, gather medication lists, and stay with the person.

Why do I need to fast before a blood test?

Fasting before certain blood tests, usually eight to twelve hours with water allowed, gives stable reference values. Recent food changes blood sugar, triglycerides and some other blood fats, which can push results outside the normal range and lead to repeat tests or wrong interpretations. Water is fine and even helpful because it keeps veins easy to find; tea and coffee without sugar are usually accepted, but check with your laboratory. Tests like lipid panels and fasting glucose are the classic ones that need it; a full blood count does not. If you take morning medication, ask your doctor whether to delay the dose until after the draw.

What is food poisoning and how quickly does it start?

Food poisoning is an illness caused by eating food contaminated with bacteria, viruses, parasites or their toxins. Onset depends on the culprit: toxins can cause vomiting within one to six hours, salmonella often takes six to 72 hours, and some bacteria like campylobacter take two to five days. Typical symptoms are nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps and diarrhoea, sometimes with fever. Most cases resolve at home with rest and steady fluids; use oral rehydration solution if diarrhoea is heavy. See a doctor for blood in stool, signs of dehydration, fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, symptoms lasting more than three days, or if the patient is pregnant, very young or elderly.

Is sun exposure really that bad for you?

Short midday exposure helps your body make vitamin D, but sunburn and chronic tanning damage skin permanently. Ultraviolet radiation is a proven human carcinogen and the main cause of skin cancer, which is the most common cancer worldwide; it also causes around 80 percent of visible facial ageing. Protect yourself with shade and clothing in the middle of the day, a broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30 reapplied every two hours, and sunglasses. Avoid tanning beds entirely. People with pale skin, many moles or a family history of skin cancer need to be stricter and check their skin regularly for new or changing spots.

What is cholesterol and should mine be low?

Cholesterol is a waxy fat your body needs to build cells and hormones; the problem is not cholesterol itself but too much LDL, the type that deposits in artery walls. High LDL over years forms plaques that narrow arteries and can rupture, causing heart attacks and strokes. HDL, the other main type, helps clear cholesterol back to the liver, so the LDL-to-HDL balance matters more than a single total number. Desirable LDL is below 3 mmol/L or about 100 mg/dL for most adults, lower if you already have heart disease or diabetes. Readings improve with less saturated fat, more fibre, exercise and not smoking; medication like statins is highly effective for people at elevated risk.

Can I drink coffee every day?

For most adults, moderate coffee of about three to four cups a day, up to roughly 400 mg of caffeine, is safe and even associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease and liver disease. Problems appear with excess: anxiety, palpitations, poor sleep and raised blood pressure for some people. Stop or cut back at least six hours before bedtime, be aware that pregnancy limits the advice to about 200 mg a day, and skip high-caffeine energy drinks. Unfiltered coffee such as French press contains cafestol which raises cholesterol slightly, so filtered coffee is the friendlier daily choice.

What is the difference between a pandemic and an epidemic?

An epidemic is a rise in cases of a disease above what is normally expected within a specific community or region. A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents, usually affecting large numbers of people; COVID-19 in 2020 is the defining recent example, while a seasonal flu outbreak in one city is an epidemic. The terms describe geography and scale, not severity. Declaring a pandemic changes the response: coordination moves to international bodies, travel and trade measures activate, and vaccine and treatment development is accelerated. The word is a signal for governments to act together, not a description of the disease itself.

How do vaccines actually work?

A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless preview of a pathogen, so it can build memory before a real infection arrives. That preview may be an inactivated virus, a weakened live virus, a piece of a protein, or genetic instructions that teach your cells to temporarily make a harmless piece of the virus, as mRNA vaccines do. Your body responds by producing antibodies and memory cells that stand ready for years or decades. If the real pathogen appears, the immune system responds fast enough to prevent severe illness. Mild fever or a sore arm after vaccination is the immune system working, not the disease itself.

What is BMI for children, is it the same as for adults?

No, children need age- and sex-specific charts. A child's body composition changes as they grow, so a BMI that is normal for a six-year-old may be concerning for a twelve-year-old; paediatricians use percentile curves rather than fixed cutoffs. A BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex defines obesity, and the 85th to 95th percentile defines overweight. The concern with childhood obesity is not appearance but trajectory: early weight gain raises the lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and fatty liver disease. Any concern about a child's weight should go through a paediatrician, because restrictive diets can harm growth.

Why does the flu come in seasons?

Seasonal patterns come from a mix of virus and human factors. Influenza viruses survive longer and spread more easily in cold, dry air, and the protective mucus layer in our airways clears less effectively in that weather. In winter people also spend more time indoors with windows shut, so droplets pass between people far more readily, and lower vitamin D levels may weaken immune defences. That is why temperate regions see flu waves in their winters while tropical regions see more year-round, rain-driven transmission. This seasonality is predictable enough that vaccine campaigns are timed months ahead of each hemisphere's season.

What should I do if someone is having a seizure?

Stay calm and time it; most seizures stop by themselves within one to two minutes. Ease the person to the floor, turn them gently onto their side to keep the airway clear, cushion the head, loosen anything tight around the neck, and move hard or sharp objects away. Never put anything in their mouth or try to hold them still. Call emergency services if it lasts longer than five minutes, if another seizure follows immediately, if the person is injured, pregnant, has never had a seizure before, or does not regain consciousness normally afterwards. Afterwards they may be confused and tired; stay with them and reassure them until fully alert.
